General Principles of Pharmacology - Pharmacokinetics

Current lecture first · official objectives control emphasis · matched prior-year note used only as reinforcement
WednesdayCore lectureQuantitative + clinical reasoningNo week symbol

Big picture: pharmacokinetics asks how the body determines drug exposure over time. The exam-facing core is the relationship among bioavailability (F), volume of distribution (Vd), clearance (Cl), half-life, and dosing, then how disease, genetics, transporters, and interacting drugs change those variables.

ObjectivesF / absorptionVdCl / eliminationKineticsDosingVariabilityInteractionsWorked caseRecall

What the official objectives actually require

1. Describe the key pharmacokinetic parameters: volume of distribution (Vd), clearance (Cl), and bioavailability (F).
2. Calculate loading and maintenance doses, including adjustment for incomplete bioavailability.
3. Distinguish first-order vs zero-order elimination and explain how Vd and Cl determine half-life.
4. List and explain major mechanisms of drug interactions.
5. Discuss implications of pharmacokinetic genetic polymorphism.
Supporting lecture context
The current deck also reviews absorption/permeation, routes of administration, protein binding, Phase I/II metabolism, and renal excretion. Those topics are included because they explain why F, Vd, and Cl change, but the five objectives above set the priority.
01Absorption and bioavailability (F)LO 1
For oral availability or central nervous system exposure, a drug must permeate a lipid bilayer or use a transporter. The deck emphasizes moderate lipophilicity, ionization, and molecular size as permeability determinants.

Permeation

Moderately lipophilic, appropriately sized, and sufficiently non-ionized drugs cross bilayers more readily.

Carrier transport

Transporters can facilitate entry or drive efflux. P-glycoprotein (P-gp) is emphasized as a barrier to gut absorption and CNS exposure.

P-glycoprotein is highlighted in the current lecture as an efflux transporter that can limit absorption and CNS exposure.
RouteCore lecture logic
OralConvenient/low risk, but requires permeation and is subject to the first-pass effect.
Sublingual / rectalCan avoid first-pass exposure.
IVRapid; permeation not needed; effectively complete systemic delivery.
IM / SCPermeation not needed; slower than IV and may provide depot exposure.
Inhaled / transdermalCan be local or systemic; systemic effects still depend on permeation.
F = fraction of administered drug reaching systemic circulation
Bioavailability: the lecture compares oral exposure to IV exposure using area under the plasma-concentration curve (AUC). Lower oral AUC means lower F.
Exam relationship
Lower F means a larger oral dose is required to deliver the same systemic amount.
02Distribution and volume of distribution (Vd)LO 1
Vd is an apparent volume, not a literal anatomical compartment. It relates the amount of drug in the body to the measured plasma concentration.
Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma drug concentration
Same drug amount, different plasma concentration: greater tissue binding lowers plasma concentration and therefore produces a larger apparent Vd.

Low Vd

Drug stays mainly in the vascular space. Large molecules and strongly protein-bound drugs tend to remain intravascular.

High Vd

Drug leaves plasma and distributes into tissues or tissue reservoirs, so measured plasma concentration is lower.

Do not memorize Vd as body water
A Vd can be larger than total body volume because it is calculated from concentration, not measured as a physical space.
Loading-dose connection
At a fixed target concentration, a larger Vd requires a larger loading dose.
03Elimination and clearance (Cl)LO 1 + 3
Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. Total clearance reflects the sum of renal, hepatic, and other clearance processes.

Kidney

Polar/hydrophilic drugs can be excreted unchanged. Renal insufficiency lowers clearance for renally eliminated drugs and often requires dosage adjustment.

Liver

Lipophilic drugs generally require metabolism to more polar products to reduce reabsorption and facilitate excretion.

Metabolic phaseCurrent-deck emphasis
Phase IOxidation by CYP enzymes; products may remain active; CYP enzymes are easily inhibited or induced.
Phase IIConjugation such as glucuronidation or acetylation; products are more chemically altered and usually inactive.
Maintenance-dose connection
Clearance controls how quickly drug must be replaced. Higher Cl generally means a higher maintenance dosing rate is needed for the same target concentration.
04First-order, zero-order, and half-lifeLO 3
First-orderZero-order
Removed per unit timeConstant fractionConstant amount
Concentration dependenceRate depends on concentrationRate no longer scales with concentration
Elimination machineryNot saturatedSaturated
Examples named in deckMost drugsPhenytoin, aspirin, ethanol
First-order elimination produces an exponential decline: the same fraction is removed during each equal time interval.
t1/2 = 0.693 × Vd / Cl

Vd goes up

Half-life goes up if clearance is unchanged.

Cl goes up

Half-life goes down if Vd is unchanged.

During continuous infusion, concentration approaches steady state as elimination rises to match the dosing rate. The approach is determined by half-life.
Fast exam move
For half-life comparisons, do not separately reason through every physiologic detail first. Start with Vd / Cl.
05Loading dose and maintenance dosingLO 2
Loading dose = Vd × target concentration
Maintenance dosing rate = Cl × target concentration
If F < 1: divide the calculated oral loading dose or dosing rate by F

Loading dose asks...

How much drug is needed to fill the apparent distribution space to the target concentration?

Maintenance asks...

How quickly must drug be replaced as clearance removes it?

Large Vd → larger loading dose. High Cl → higher maintenance rate. Low F → larger oral dose/rate.
Example of incomplete F
If F = 0.5, only half the administered dose reaches systemic circulation, so the oral dose needed for the same systemic target is doubled.
06Pharmacokinetic variability and genetic polymorphismLO 5
The current lecture names several patient factors that can move pharmacokinetic parameters: genetic variability in CYP expression, renal/hepatic/cardiac insufficiency, age-related changes in body composition, edema, and bowel disease.
FactorParameter most directly emphasized
CYP genotype / enzyme expressionF and/or Cl through altered metabolism
Renal/hepatic/cardiac insufficiencyCl
Older age / lower muscle massVd
EdemaVd
Bowel diseaseF
Warfarin is used in the lecture as a pharmacogenetic example: metabolism and drug target biology can both contribute to dose variability.
The lecture shows genotype-dependent warfarin dose requirements, reinforcing that inherited variation can produce clinically meaningful dose differences.
Matched prior-year note - use as reinforcement, not scope expansion
The earlier note also used warfarin to connect metabolic genotype to clearance and dose. The current lecture values and examples control if an older note differs.
07Drug interactions: three mechanisms to recognizeLO 4

1. CYP inhibition / induction

Changes metabolism and therefore drug exposure and clearance.

2. P-gp inhibition / induction

Changes efflux, especially across gut and CNS barriers, altering absorption/exposure.

3. Plasma protein displacement

Changes the free fraction of highly bound drugs.

Clinical consequence

The direction of the effect depends on whether the interacting drug inhibits or induces the pathway and whether the affected drug is a substrate.

Current-deck example of dose adjustment when poor-metabolizer status and CYP inhibitors/inducers alter drug exposure.
Reasoning pattern
Identify the substrate → identify inhibition vs induction → predict exposure, clearance, and toxicity/therapeutic-failure direction.
08Lecture worked problem: integrate the parametersLO 1-4
Current lecture example problem comparing Drug A and Drug B. Use the current table values shown here; do not import older-year numbers.
QuestionHow to reason from the current table
Which drug has the longer half-life?Compare Vd / Cl. Drug A: 180 L with 45 mL/min; Drug B: 10 L with 90 mL/min. Drug A has the larger ratio and longer half-life.
Which more likely needs renal-failure adjustment?Look at percent excreted unchanged. Drug A (>95%) is much more dependent on renal elimination.
Which more likely undergoes CYP metabolism?Only 1% of Drug B is excreted unchanged, so Drug B is much more likely to require metabolism before excretion.
Which is retained in the vascular compartment?Drug B: 98% protein bound and Vd 10 L versus Drug A Vd 180 L.
Current-vs-old source guard
The matched prior-year note used different hypothetical numbers. For this course build, the values in the current Class of 2030 lecture are authoritative.
09Closed-note recall checklistFinal pass

Can you say these without notes?

  • What F, Vd, and Cl each mean.
  • Why P-gp can lower oral/CNS exposure.
  • Why Vd can exceed body volume.
  • First-order vs zero-order.
  • t1/2 relationship to Vd and Cl.

Can you calculate / predict these?

  • Loading dose from Vd and target.
  • Maintenance rate from Cl and target.
  • How to correct either for F<1.
  • How renal disease changes a renally cleared drug.
  • How CYP/P-gp inhibition or induction changes exposure.
Four equations / relationships
Vd = amount / concentration · t1/2 = 0.693(Vd)/Cl · loading = Vd × target / F · maintenance rate = Cl × target / F
